title: Electronic reminders coming soon for Portage County jurors, defendants
author: Wendy Di Alesandro
description: The Portage County Action Team is observing its fifth anniversary with a win.
content:
The Portage County Action Team is observing its fifth anniversary with a win.
For years, PCAT members have been lobbying county leaders to send out emails and text message reminders to jurors and defendants. The county court system's outdated computer system wouldn't allow such reminders, but an update is in the final stages.
Portage County Common Pleas Court Judge Lori Pittman said a text reminder protocol for jurors should be up and running in six weeks. The county's IT department anticipates text message and email reminder systems for defendants should be online in about six months, she said.
'We're trying to get into the 21st century,' she said.
PCAT started in 2020 when Portage County NAACP Criminal Justice Chair Kathy Kerns and ACLU of Ohio Senior Organizing Strategist Melekte Melaku met at an ACLU Cleveland town hall about pretrial detention and pretrial justice.
The pair formed PCAT, which the ACLU sponsors, to support bail reform legislation and broader criminal legal system reforms. In past years, the PCAT has lobbied Ohio legislators in support of pretrial justice, launched a Civic School public education program, held bail reform teach-ins and virtual voter empowerment town halls, and shed light on criminal/legal fines and fees.
Members include the county NAACP chapter; community activist Frank Hairston; county Treasurer John Kennedy; Arie Goodman of the Ohio TroubleNation group Advocates, Allies & Activists; Kent State University students; League of Women Voters (Kent); the drug treatment organization Open United Recovery; and others.
Partnering with the NAACP, LWV (Kent) and Advocates, Allies & Activists, PCAT last year co-sponsored a program outlining the power and scope of county sheriffs. They have also sponsored a Know Your Rights community forum and another about gun laws.
Melaku and Kerns spoke with Portage County Municipal Court Judge Kevin Poland, who mentioned that electronic pretrial reminder systems might significantly reduce the number of defendants who fail to show up for court.
'This is an idea that has been used in other courts, and it's an idea that we've talked about for some time,' Poland said. 'When someone fails to appear, then our only option is to issue a warrant for their arrest. They get picked up, they may be held for a day or two or three days, which could put their job in jeopardy, which could cascade to a whole slew of ramifications.'
People shouldn't have to spend time behind bars simply because of nonappearance, Melaku said.
Pittman said she prefers pretrial email reminders because, in her experience, people change their phone numbers more often than they do their emails. Email, or maybe even snail mail, may be more effective and cost-efficient options, she said.
Melaku, though, said that it is an assumption that people regularly check their email. And Poland noted that no system will work well if defendants provide incorrect phone numbers and/or email addresses. It happens, he said.
The new reminder system, in whatever form or forms it takes, can't launch soon enough for either Melaku or Kerns.
Kerns said electronic reminders do more than help defendants keep their court dates and reduce instances of prosecutors, public defenders and court staff having to reschedule those dates. Such systems would also benefit the Portage County Sheriff's Office, whose deputies would potentially be dispatched less often to execute warrants for nonappearance, she added.
'It's just a win-win, right? Who loses?' Kerns asked. 'Every little tiny medical office has a text reminder system. Everybody has text reminders now. You don't need to be a big corporation to have that.'
PCAT also supports the ACLU's efforts to waive pretrial electronic monitors, overreliance on cash bail and what Melaku terms 'the criminalization of poverty at the municipal and county level.'

title: Op-ed: Future patients deserve access to Medicaid
author: Noyonikaa Gupta
description: At the end of 2024, the state of Ohio proposed changes to Medicaid eligibility that would require people between the ages of 19 and 55 to prove they are employed in order to receive coverage.
content:
By Noyonikaa Gupta (M1) and Shannon Lam (M2), Northeast Ohio Medical University
Please note that all opinions expressed are strictly our own and do not represent the medical school that we attend.
At the end of 2024, the state of Ohio proposed changes to Medicaid eligibility that would require people between the ages of 19 and 55 to prove they are employed in order to receive coverage. These new work requirements is projected to strip over 60,000 Ohioans of healthcare coverage. The state claims that, overall, the new requirements will encourage sustained employment and that health outcomes will improve due to an increase in one's personal involvement and engagement with their healthcare because of employment and/or education (Ohio Department of Medicaid). Similar efforts in other states around the country have been largely unsuccessful; Arkansas spent more money on administration than they would have had they just maintained coverage. It did not push more people into the workforce, but rather became another significant barrier to receiving healthcare for those who need it most. In fact, in 2013, Ohio governor John Kasich described Medicaid expansion through the Affordable Care Act as a 'matter of life and death.'
While Portage County has an unemployment rate that is well below the national value (4.5% versus 5.0%), unemployment and underemployment are still issues that the population faces. In fact, in 2023 the OhioMeansJobs (OMJ) Portage County Center saw an overall increase in utilization of services in addition to taking on over 350 new customers. The OMJ served over 1800 total customers in 2023. This demonstrates that citizens are still committed to finding work and/or finding jobs that better suit their qualifications and goals. And, in 2023, Portage County 'met and exceeded the 90% of Medicaid renewals completed during all countable months' (2023 Portage County Annual Report), which shows just how valuable Medicaid services and resources are to the citizens of Portage County.
Stripping Medicaid access from citizens suffering from illness and disease inevitably prevents them from receiving vital healthcare and keeps them out of the workforce for even longer–a counterproductive measure. Low-income individuals who rely on Medicaid are more likely to have language barriers or lack of access to internet services that will make it more difficult to prove their employment and prevent them from having access to insurance. Access to quality healthcare is a human right, and creating barriers and unequal access widens health disparities. As concerned medical students, we believe that the newly proposed Medicaid work requirements will harm Ohioans. Medicaid provides access to necessary mental health services and helps lower medical debt. Our future patients deserve better. Our future patients deserve access to healthcare regardless of their work or financial status.

title: Around Brimfield: Egg free baking, plus news and events in Brimfield
author: Shirley Mars
description: How do chickens stay fit? They eggs-ercise! Speaking of chickens, is anyone else wondering what egg-actly is going on with the price of eggs? After some eggs-haustive research, I am still not an egg…
content:
How do chickens stay fit? They eggs-ercise! Speaking of chickens, is anyone else wondering what egg-actly is going on with the price of eggs? After some eggs-haustive research, I am still not an egg-spert, but let me try to eggs-plain what I have learned.
First, I learned that Ohio leads the nation in bird flu cases. Fewer chickens equals fewer eggs. That is not good.
Secondly, eggs tend to be a 'loss leader' which is a common business strategy where inexpensive items are priced under wholesale with the goal to get customers to buy other higher profit items while they are at the store. Two examples from Costco are the $1.50 hot dog and drink deal and their $4.99 rotisserie chickens.
Thirdly, there are risks to loss leader pricing, such as some customers who only buy loss leaders and then shop elsewhere for other items or when customers buy so much of a loss leader that supplies run out. In the case of eggs, supplies are running low, thus limits are being placed on them.
For those who get upset with restaurants for adding surcharges or raising their prices, keep in mind that they do not operate on a loss leader strategy, thus they are likely paying more for wholesale eggs, and the egg crisis may continue to be egg-stremely frustrating with even higher prices. Something that we can be egg-cited about is that there are still fresh egg stands throughout Brimfield.
If you do not have an egg to crack, desperation can lead to inspiration. I have listed a few egg-cellent replacements for egg-free baking. Each egg can be replaced with either ¼ C mashed banana, applesauce, pumpkin puree, yogurt or buttermilk or by mixing 1 Tbsp. ground flaxseed with 3 Tbsp. water. Also, combining 1 Tbsp. of vinegar and 1 tsp. of baking soda creates a chemical reaction that releases carbon dioxide, replacing the leavening typically achieved with eggs to produce light and airy baked goods. title: Astoria's Bizzell wins state swimming title
author: Paul Matli The Astorian
description: It's been nearly 50 years since the Astoria High School swimming program debuted during the 1978-1979 season.
content:
It's been nearly 50 years since the Astoria High School swimming program debuted during the 1978-1979 season.
Now, the program has its first state champion.
Finn Bizzell cemented his legacy as the greatest swimmer in Astoria High School history on Saturday, Feb. 22, as he won the state title in the 50-yard freestyle at the 4A/3A/2A/1A State Swimming Championships in Beaverton.
Not only did Bizzell win the title, he set a new school record in the process. His time of 22.01 was one of three school records set by the senior at the state meet. The others came in the 100-yard butterfly and 400-yard freestyle relay.
Bizzell finished fourth in the 100 butterfly and broke his previous record in the event by swimming the race in 53.59. He wrapped up his Astoria career by posting a 100-yard relay split time of 48.53.
After his performance on Saturday Bizzell owns four of the eight school records for the boys team.
Bizzell wasn't the only Astoria swimmer to post terrific times during the state meet. Senior Hazel Towsey-French set three personal best times during her 500-yard freestyle race.
Towsey-French finished in 11th place with a time of 6:00.45, an improvement of 6.5 seconds from her previous best time. Paul Gascoigne, the team's head coach, said Towsey-French posted personal best times at both the 100- and 200-yard points of the race.
The Fishermen also brought two relay teams to state and saw improved finishes.
The Astoria boys 200-yard freestyle relay team of John Ero, Gabe White, Casey Dopp and Bizzell came into the weekend seeded 12th and ended up improving one spot to 11th, after dropping two seconds from their previous season-best time.
The boys 400 freestyle relay team followed a similar script, as they came in seeded 11th and improved to 10th. The foursome consisting of Bizzell, Sam Reid, Dopp and Ero dropped 8.63 seconds from their previous season-best time.
Astoria boys finished tied for 10th overall in the team competition with Bizzell scoring all their points.

content:
Our hero D. Jeffrey 'Jeff' Miller passed away peacefully at the age of 63, after his hard fought 8-year battle with brain cancer, on Wednesday, February 26, 2025, with his family lovingly by his side. Born on August 27, 1961, in Ravenna, Ohio; he was a lifelong resident of Windham, Ohio.
He is survived by his loving wife, Lisa Crews Miller; mother, Janet Priddy Miller; sister, Amy Miller Olson; children, Corey (Christina) Miller, Lauren (Justin) Miller, Mackenzie (Angel) Miller, Emily (Zakery) Rowe and Nicole (Joshua) Sweet; grandchildren, Elisabeth, Madison, DJ Miller, Ayla Corzine, Blake & Easton Miller, Teagan Goetz, Mackenzie Chaffin, Spencer, JJ & Noah Sweet; in-laws, Phillip & Sarah Crews and sister-in-law, Teresa (Jim) Hardgrove; along with many aunts, uncles, cousins, and friends.
He is preceded in death by his father, Donald Miller; we know they are together playing 18-holes of golf, celebrating their reunion.
Jeff graduated from Windham High School in 1979, and he was a friend to every person he met. He had the ability to make everyone feel seen and valued. Jeff was always ready with a helping hand and a listening ear. Jeff was known to share one of his many stories over a cup of sugar with his coffee, offer support during difficult times, and simply brighten someone's day with a smile. Jeff lived a life dedicated to connecting with others. He loved playing golf, bowling, hunting, fishing and he loved to sing and dance. Jeff was his children's biggest teacher, mentor and coach and their number 1 fan; he never missed a single sport game or event and was always there to cheer and whistle them on. Jeff was a huge Cleveland Guardians and Dallas Cowboys fan and loved to umpire little league games. He will be remembered as a beloved son and brother, devoted husband, loving dad, and reliable friend; but Jeff's best role was proud Papaw.
Jeff will be deeply missed by family, friends, and the entire community, and his memory will live on in the hearts of those whose lives he touched and through the legacy of this humility he leaves and his cherished family. A special thank you to the wonderful staff at Tamarack Ridge and Suma Hospice for loving Jeff so fiercely the last six months.
A Celebration of Life will be held Saturday, March 8, 2025, at Windham United Methodist Church, 9051 N. Main Street, Windham, Ohio. Visitation starts at 12:00 pm followed by the Celebration of Life at 1:00 pm. After the service, friends and family are invited to gather for a luncheon to share fond memories and stories together and celebrate his life.
In lieu of flowers, please send donations to Windham Youth Baseball and Softball Organization to WYBSO P.O. Box 391, Windham OH 44288.

title: Letter: Not a sucker or a loser
description: Frederick White re Donald Trump and Russia
content:
I am a veteran of the Cold War, in which I was a mechanic on a missile launch crew on Okinawa, and then in Montana as support staff in shops which serviced a large Minuteman Missile complex.

title: Streetsboro seeks to honor Chuck Kocisko's legacy, Family Days cancelled and more
author: Staff Report
description: People close to Charles 'Chuck' Kocisko — and those who only knew his reputation as a public servant of Streetsboro — have shared their appreciation and condolences following his death in January.
content:
People close to Charles 'Chuck' Kocisko — and those who only knew his reputation as a public servant of Streetsboro — have shared their appreciation and condolences following his death in January.
'Chuck did an enormous amount of things for the city,' Mayor Glenn Broska said. 'He was one of the founding fathers of Streetsboro Junior Baseball back in the day. He basically committed his off time to serving the city.'
Kocisko, a former City Council member and the founder of Streetsboro Family Days, died on Jan. 9 at age 83. City leaders plan to honor his contributions with street and baseball field dedications and by taking on a greater role with community events.
'He always had family and community at heart and put them first.' 'Our lives are better because he was in it,' read online tributes at Shorts-Spicer-Crislip Funeral Homes.
'I don't recall meeting Chuck, but his influence throughout the city has been felt in virtually every fiber of its goings on for decades,' a comment on Facebook stated.
A statement posted to the Streetsboro Family Days' website and Facebook page in early February announced the cancellation of this year's four-day festival, which is typically hosted in July by a small group of families at Streetsboro City Park.
'We need this time to heal, take time for ourselves and reflect on the future of Streetsboro Family Days,' it stated.
Messages to Von Starkey, president of the nonprofit event board and Kocisko's daughter, were not returned.
Community members have gathered for concerts, fair food and other entertainment at Streetsboro Family Days since 2003. However, that attendance noticeably declined when the ride operator was not available in recent years, Broska and Councilman Jon Hannan said.
'I've always attended Family Days,' Hannan said. 'I've always enjoyed it, but I know that attendance has declined just because of the fair not having any rides, and that was out of their control.'
Last summer, the city coordinated its inaugural Brew & BBQ Bash. The one-day event featured a barbecue competition and craft brewers and was a 'resounding success,' Broska said.
The Parks and Recreation event coordinator helped plan it but, to avoid using taxpayer money, the city worked with the nonprofit Streetsboro Heritage Foundation to collect donations and pay vendors. Broska said the city plans to host the event again and add additional festivals, especially once the 'Gateway Green' or city center project is complete.
An ordinance, which will be up for a final council vote March 10, would add a new section to the city's administrative code related to city-sponsored events. It would give the event coordinator authority to seek sponsorships and enter concession agreements and designate a fund for those purposes.
'It is our desire to offer the different programs and stuff on the Gateway Green that other communities around us have,' Broska said. 'I think it's important that we have that to build a sense of place and to build a sense of community.'
Hannan said the legislation will keep finances 'transparent' and ensure that event funds do not take money from roads or other essential city services.
'It basically creates a separate account so then that way, when that money comes in from sponsorships, it gives us flexibility of using that money for city-sponsored events,' he said.
City Council on Feb. 24 also approved the dedication of the northeast Public Square Road as 'Chuck Kocisko Way.' Members also intend to name the baseball fields at Streetsboro City Park after Kocisko but are debating whether it should be dubbed 'ball fields' or 'athletic complex.'
Hannan, who played Streetsboro Junior Baseball & Softball growing up, said Kocisko's contributions as former president of the organization included lights and dugouts at the fields. He considered Kocisko a mentor while serving alongside him on City Council from 2017 to 2021 — when Kocisko lost his re-election bid — and continued to seek his advice afterward.
Kocisko, a U.S. Army veteran, had previously served on City Council and also served on the city's Planning Commission, Streetsboro Visitors & Convention Bureau and Streetsboro Area Chamber of Commerce. Hannan said his community knowledge was 'like a Streetsboro history book.'
'I think his contributions to the city were huge, and I think it's just truly fitting to name something after him,' Hannan said.

title: Ohio Outdoors: Winging into spring
author: Julie Watson
description: It's March, and spring is in the air, literally. No matter if the month came in like a lion or a lamb, look and listen to the skies for vernal evidence. Harbingers of spring are winging their way…
content:
It's March, and spring is in the air, literally. No matter if the month came in like a lion or a lamb, look and listen to the skies for vernal evidence. Harbingers of spring are winging their way north as you read this. And no, I'm not talking about robins. Robins don't actually migrate; they stay in Portage County year-round. So that 'first robin of spring' sighting isn't something to get all worked up about.
However, in the past two weeks I have seen and heard flocks of Sandhill Cranes, Trumpeter Swans, Turkey Vultures, and most exciting of all, blackbirds. Now, blackbirds may not seem all that great but keep reading and you'll find out why they are.
There are many species of blackbirds, Brewer's, Grackles, and Cowbirds, just to name a few. They are generally black to brown, medium sized, perching birds, and they stick together. Many different types of blackbirds will congregate and travel together in large flocks during migration; after all, there is safety in numbers. Blackbirds are so gregarious they will even flock with European Starlings from time to time.
But the reason it's so exciting to see blackbirds in Portage County this time of year is because of one species in particular: Agelaius phoeniceus , more commonly known as the red-winged blackbird. These are the true sign of spring, and last week, I saw two of them!
The females and immature males are slightly larger than sparrows with similar markings. This provides excellent camouflage amongst the cattails and marsh grasses where they nest. As with most bird species, mature males are showier than the others. Males of breeding age are glossy black with a patch of red at the top of the wing called an epaulet. Sometimes these epaulets are concealed revealing only the yellow stripe that underlines the red.
OK, so with all these visual obstacles, how do you know if red-winged blackbirds have returned to usher in spring? This is where listening comes in. Red-wings have a very musical call with notes that sound like running water. It is easily recognized. In fact, it's one of my favorite bird calls (right behind most owl calls). Check it out: Red-winged Blackbird Sounds, All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology.
Males call to attract mates and defend their territory. Their sound can be heard in marshy areas and among farmland all summer long. In fact, some would argue that in addition to crickets, red-wing blackbird calls are the sound of summer.
When those cold March winds blow and snowflakes are flying, it's easy to doubt that spring is right around the corner. Remember, all you have to do is look and listen to the skies for proof that spring is on the way.
If you'd like to be able to identify birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, a world leader in wild bird research and identification developed the Merlin App. The App went live in 2014. It is free and runs on both Apple and Android devices. Happy birding!
As spring approaches all of our feathered friends could use a little help. Here's what you can do: Fill the feeders
Provide fresh water
Provide shelter from weather and predators
Keep cats away
Put up nest boxes
Put bits of string, yarn, hair and fur out in your yard for nesting materials

title: Guest Column: Oregon should not follow Congress on corporate tax subsidies
author: Juan Carlos Ordóñez
description: When it comes to tax policy, all too often Oregon fails to fly with her own wings. Rather than heed her motto, Oregon hitches a ride on the back of
content:
When it comes to tax policy, all too often Oregon fails to fly with her own wings. Rather than heed her motto, Oregon hitches a ride on the back of Congress, no matter how awful the destination.
Right now, Congress is heading toward handing corporations several tax cuts that would accomplish little other than pad corporate profits. These wasteful tax cuts would automatically become Oregon law, sapping hundreds of millions of dollars from the current state budget that could instead be used to invest in Oregonians — unless Oregon lawmakers vote to stop it.

title: Letter: Correlated

content:

This timber harvest, the Tippy Top Sort Sale, authorizes 58 acres of the drinking watershed to undergo variable retention harvest. Stimson Lumber Co. and Hampton Tree Farms were the highest bidders for harvest. With expenses of logging services from JWN Trucking and road work from Warrenton Fiber Co., the city will earn half a million dollars in revenue.

title: Letter: Wasted
description: Colin Cummings re U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden's town hall
content:
When I realized I had missed U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden's town hall event in Astoria, I was disappointed. When I read about how the war in Gaza dominated the event, I was angry that I didn't attend.
It's worth pointing out how accessible Wyden makes himself, and what a real opportunity it is, as citizens, to be able to speak to one of our senators directly. As a previous resident of Texas, I can tell you that U.S. senators are not accessible to most Americans; we Oregonians are fortunate.

description: The Daily Morning Astorian, on March 31, 1885, mentions that Capt. Amlot brought the steamer Barrowmore in with extra souls aboard who had been picked up at sea on Jan.
content:
The Daily Morning Astorian, on March 31, 1885, mentions that Capt. Amlot brought the steamer Barrowmore in with extra souls aboard who had been picked up at sea on Jan. 25. They were the captain and crew of the Kirkwood, who had narrowly escaped death.
Before the Barrowmore arrived, the steamer Germanic came across the Kirkwood, which was dismasted and taking on water. The Germanic's captain inexplicably refused to take the Kirkwood's crew aboard, oblivious to the fact that the vessel was sinking despite frantic pumping efforts.

title: Letter: Everyday heroes
description: Cindy Colley re everyday heroes
content:
Recently, I was in Pelican Brewing Co. in Cannon Beach and witnessed a most amazing rescue. The lobby was packed to the point that a person could hardly move. People were standing. All the benches were full.
Meghan Welsh, a hostess, was coming around the podium to call names for folks whose tables were ready. She had her iPad in her right hand as she rounded the podium. A toddler, who was standing on the edge of the bench, lost his balance and started to fall. The toddler was falling headfirst and would have landed on his head.

author: Elleda Wilson The Astorian
description: In late March, a brilliant red, translucent 2-pound rock was found on Short Beach, near Oceanside, by Matt Ransom, of Portland, who was walking with his wife, Lani, according to
content:
In late March, a brilliant red, translucent 2-pound rock was found on Short Beach, near Oceanside, by Matt Ransom, of Portland, who was walking with his wife, Lani, according to a Yahoo News story.
A geologist from the Oregon Department of Geology and Mineral Industries, Mike Darin, took a look at it. 'The rich red color, translucence, texture and lack of banding suggest it is a carnelian,' he said. ' ... As for the interesting shape, it looks to have been formed by natural processes of erosion ... '

title: Letter: The world is ending
description: Roger Dorband re climate change
content:
Some of the wisest teachers I have had the privilege to learn from state flatly that because of climate change the world is ending, or at least our world, as we have known it. How it ends will be very much up to us. We have many choices in front of us but not this one — that the world we know is ending; the framework by which we have lived is ending.
The new order of things will require relinquishment, simplicity, community and becoming downwardly mobile. These traits, anathema to most Americans, will most likely come as the result of great collective suffering, but not necessarily so. We simply need to develop a sense of hope based on a vision of a brave new world in order to transition beyond the trouble we are in.

title: Weekend Break: 'Swamp Concerto'
author: Patrick Webb
description: A couple who live next to a delicate Lower Columbia River ecosystem have found a way to highlight its importance through art.
content:
A couple who live next to a delicate Lower Columbia River ecosystem have found a way to highlight its importance through art.
Anna Daedalus and Kerry Davis will display their unusual designs at an exhibit in Astoria opening this weekend.
Patrick Webb is a former managing editor of The Astorian.

title: Ocean salmon season recommendations announced
author: The Astorian
description: The Pacific Fishery Management Council has finalized its 2024 ocean salmon season recommendations.
content:
The Pacific Fishery Management Council has finalized its 2024 ocean salmon season recommendations.
Recommended salmon seasons are not official until final approval by the National Marine Fisheries Service, expected by May 16, and after adoption in April by the Oregon Fish and Wildlife Commission for waters within 3 nautical miles of shore.

title: One lane of W. Marine Drive closes for sewer repairs
author: The Astorian
description: One lane of a section of W. Marine Drive closed Wednesday for repairs to a collapsed sewer main.
content:
One lane of a section of W. Marine Drive closed Wednesday for repairs to a collapsed sewer main.
The closure, which impacts the eastbound right lane between Hamburg Avenue and Portway Street, is expected to continue through Thursday or until work is completed.

title: County commission candidates emphasize cost of living, habitat conservation plan at election forum
author: Olivia Palmer The Astorian
description: Scheller and Huacuja are campaigning for the District 2 seat on the county Board of Commissioners
content:
Candidates for District 2 on the Clatsop County Board of Commissioners weighed in on a range of issues at an election forum Tuesday night at Clatsop Community College in Astoria, from the cost of living and vacation rentals to the state's habitat conservation plan.
The forum — moderated by former Astoria Mayor Arline LaMear and presented by the American Association of University Women's Astoria Branch, The Astorian and Coast Community Radio — comes just over a month from the May 21 election.

title: Miami softball extends record-breaking win streak to 21 games
author: Addison Lenhart
description: Miami softball continued its historically dominant season on Tuesday afternoon, sweeping Ball State in a doubleheader. The RedHawks' 8-3 and 5-4 victories over the Cardinals extended Miami's win…
content:
Miami softball continued its historically dominant season on Tuesday afternoon, sweeping Ball State in a doubleheader. The RedHawks' 8-3 and 5-4 victories over the Cardinals extended Miami's win streak to 21 consecutive games, a Mid-American Conference record.
Miami softball continued its historically dominant season on Tuesday afternoon, sweeping Ball State in a doubleheader. The RedHawks' 8-3 and 5-4 victories over the Cardinals extended Miami's win streak to 21 consecutive games, a Mid-American Conference record. Sixth-year catcher Allie Cummins came up huge for the RedHawks in both contests, homering twice in game one, and putting another on the board for some insurance in the sixth inning of game two.

'Today I was seeing the ball a little bit better and I was able to put good swings on it,' Cummins said. 'Always happy when that happens.'

Kate Kobayashi went deep in game 1 and Holly Blaska added another homer in game 2 which brings Miami's team total to 118 home runs on the season, which leads the country by 24.

'We know that if we struggle one day somebody's gonna be there to have our back,' Cummins said. 'The streak happens because we all have the same goal. It allows us to have a little more fun than other teams who rely on two or three hitters.'

Madilyn Reeves and Ashley Jarvis both went the distance in each of their starts, allowing a combined five runs and striking out nine batters. Kumar's RedHawks have been dominant ever since she arrived on campus in 2021. However, this season the RedHawks are off to a start that tops even her first three seasons, as they've sprinted out to a 34-6 record through 40 games and found themselves ranked 24th in the country beginning this week. Kumar says despite all the success, her team's focus hasn't wavered.

title: Warrenton baseball continues their win streak
author: Paul Matli The Astorian
description: After falling behind 1-0, the Warrenton Warriors baseball team scored the last seven runs of the game to cruise to a 7-1 victory. Odin Wilson started, went six innings and
content:
After falling behind 1-0, the Warrenton Warriors baseball team scored the last seven runs of the game to cruise to a 7-1 victory. Odin Wilson started, went six innings and struck out 10 batters.
Cam'Ron Daniels came in to relieve Wilson at the top of the seventh inning, and got out of a bases loaded, nobody out jam. Daniels had a strikeout and induced a double play ball to end the game.

title: In One Ear: Hawaiian Chieftain sails again
author: Elleda Wilson
description: On April 10, the Peninsula Daily News in Washington had a short snippet about a vessel that once sailed the Columbia River:
content:
On April 10, the Peninsula Daily News in Washington had a short snippet about a vessel that once sailed the Columbia River:
'The Hawaiian Chieftain, a 103-foot sailing ship, was returned to the water Tuesday after it spent several years being restored at the Port of Port Townsend Boat Haven. The ship, purchased from the Grays Harbor Historical Society by Aubrey and Matt Wilson, will now return to Hawaii, where it will be available for tours and events.'

title: Fabiano joins Foot & Ankle Clinic
author: Erica Fabiano
description: The Columbia Memorial Hospital — Oregon Health & Science University Health Foot & Ankle Clinic has welcomed Erica Fabiano, an advanced practice nurse practitioner, as a new provider.
content:
The Columbia Memorial Hospital — Oregon Health & Science University Health Foot & Ankle Clinic has welcomed Erica Fabiano, an advanced practice nurse practitioner, as a new provider.
Fabiano most recently worked as a nurse practitioner at the University of Iowa Hospital and Clinics in the Emergency General Surgery and Trauma Unit in Iowa City, Iowa. She earned a doctorate of nursing practice from Clarke University in Dubuque, Iowa, and is certified by the American Nurses Credentialing Center.

title: Letter: Doubly thankful
description: Merianne Myers re Tessa Scheller for Clatsop County Board of Commissioners
content:
I am always grateful that I get to vote. It's a connection to the big "all of us" that is hard to come by on an every day basis.
Yes, elections have been tedious and annoying, and even scary over the past few years. But in May, we have an opportunity to vote, and know our vote counts large in a small electorate. I am doubly thankful that Tessa Scheller has stepped up to run for Clatsop County commissioner in District 2.

title: Letter: Great opportunity
description: Sue Cody re Tessa Scheller for Clatsop County Board of Commissioners
content:
Clatsop County has a great opportunity to keep this place healthy, economically viable and welcoming to everyone by electing Tessa Scheller to the Clatsop County commission, District 2.
Tessa has the background and knowledge of county matters from serving on multiple boards, including Clatsop Community College, among others.

title: In One Ear: Clever corps
author: Elleda Wilson
description: For informational diversion with a humorous twist, go visit the Portland District, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Facebook page. They're the clever folks who bring you the annual cat and
content:
For informational diversion with a humorous twist, go visit the Portland District, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Facebook page. They're the clever folks who bring you the annual cat and dog calendars featuring oversized pets lounging on, or playing with dams, ships, etc., and the photo shown (corps' caption added).
The page encourages interaction, saying they're 'always just a DM (direct message) away!' Some of the exchanges are particularly silly, especially when a 'bot' named Elna started getting fresh.

title: In One Ear: Enduring appeal
author: Elleda Wilson The Astorian
description: On Saturday, the gold pocket watch belonging to John Jacob Astor IV, great-grandson of Astoria's namesake, and found on his body after the sinking of the Titanic on April 15,
content:
On Saturday, the gold pocket watch belonging to John Jacob Astor IV, great-grandson of Astoria's namesake, and found on his body after the sinking of the Titanic on April 15, 1912, was auctioned off by Henry Aldridge & Son Ltd. in England.
The watch was expected to fetch between about $126,000 and $190,000 at auction, but wound up selling for the astonishing sum of close to $1.5 million, The Guardian reported.

title: Letter: Shoutout
description: Eric Macdonald re Clatsop Care Memory Community
content:
A shoutout to the Clatsop Care Memory Community staff. Like all caregiving positions, the memory community staff begins with intrinsic qualities like love, patience and kindness. Time brings the extrinsic skills of caring for our challenging residents.
The staff are hardworking and amazing. But they have families to feed, and wages are no longer competitive. They are leaving. And job hunters are not looking for hard work for less pay.

title: 'We didn't walk away'
author: Rebecca Norden-Bright
description: Transit district gradually restores bus service one year after financial collapse
content:
A year after a financial collapse shut down bus service on the North Coast, bus ridership in the Sunset Empire Transportation District remains less than half of what it was before the disruption.
Monthly figures shared by the transit district show gradual progress toward restoring service, but, as of the end of March, the district was providing several thousand fewer rides compared to March 2023.

title: Urology Clinic announces improved imaging for prostate cancer patients
author: The Astorian
description: The Columbia Memorial Hospital — Oregon Health & Science University Health Urology Clinic is now able to offer men with prostate cancer targeted positron emission tomography imaging with Pylarify, an
content:
The Columbia Memorial Hospital — Oregon Health & Science University Health Urology Clinic is now able to offer men with prostate cancer targeted positron emission tomography imaging with Pylarify, an imaging agent approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to identify suspected metastasis or a return of prostate cancer.
"Prostate cancer imaging plays a vital role in helping to detect and monitor prostate cancer progression," Dr. Grecori Anderson, of the Urology Clinic, said in a statement. "There are several types of imaging tests, but not all imaging scans are the same. Using Pylarify will give us a better image of where the prostate cancer is, helping us work with our patients for more informed treatment choices."

title: Recall holds as ballots counted for rural fire district board
author: Jasmine Lewin
description: With last-minute ballots counted in the recall election, three board members of the Elsie-Vinemaple Rural Fire Protection District are out and a fourth was holding on by three votes.
content:
With last-minute ballots counted in the recall election, three board members of the Elsie-Vinemaple Rural Fire Protection District are out and a fourth was holding on by three votes.
Board chair Vivian McCann and board members Wayne Carmichael and Staciy Morrison were recalled. Board member Thomas Hecox was maintaining his position.

title: Everyday People: At Recology, Hammond woman finds path to success
author: Julia Eastham The Astorian
description: Katie Hardesty, the operations manager at Recology Western Oregon, knows just about everything about trash and recycle pickup across the North Coast.
content:
Katie Hardesty, the operations manager at Recology Western Oregon, knows just about everything about trash and recycle pickup across the North Coast.
Recology, a San Francisco, California, based waste management and recycling company, has been Hardesty's employer for over a decade. The single mother of two began her journey at the company as a driver after moving to Hammond from the McMinnville area.

title: Recreational fishing days added along river
author: The Astorian
description: During a joint state hearing Wednesday following an update on anticipated upstream returns, fishery managers from Oregon and Washington state added 10 additional days for recreational spring Chinook fishing downstream
content:
During a joint state hearing Wednesday following an update on anticipated upstream returns, fishery managers from Oregon and Washington state added 10 additional days for recreational spring Chinook fishing downstream of Bonneville Dam.
Fishery biologists are now expecting a return of 122,400 upriver-origin adult Chinook, similar to the preseason forecast of 121,000.

title: In One Ear: Still ticking
author: Elleda Wilson The Astorian
description: The buyer of John Jacob Astor IV‘s 14-karat engraved gold watch for $1.5 million at a Henry Aldridge & Son auction in April is as interesting as Astor himself. Astor,
content:
The buyer of John Jacob Astor IV ‘s 14-karat engraved gold watch for $1.5 million at a Henry Aldridge & Son auction in April is as interesting as Astor himself. Astor, great-grandson of Astoria's namesake, was one of the wealthiest men in the U.S. at the time of the Titanic's demise on April 15, 1912, and was well known as a real estate magnate and author.
Patrick Gruhn, the winning bidder, is a German entrepreneur and lawyer. Off to an early start, he founded his first information technology startup at 18 in Germany. Now based in Oregon, his LinkedIn profile says he lives in Portland, and is now CEO of PMX Technologies (Kephas Corp.) in Florence. He is also the founder of the startup Perpetuals.com Group for cryptocurrency trading, which he is getting ready for launch.

title: In One Ear: Convocation of eagles
author: Elleda Wilson The Astorian
description: 'The bald eagles have been out in force,' the Seaside Aquarium posted May 10 on Facebook. 'Driving from Gearhart to the South Jetty we counted over 17!'
content:
'The bald eagles have been out in force,' the Seaside Aquarium posted May 10 on Facebook. 'Driving from Gearhart to the South Jetty we counted over 17!'
Worldwide, there are only eight species of sea eagles, the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife says, and the bald eagle is the only one found throughout North America. As far as Oregon goes, the bald eagle breeds in 32 of the 36 counties, and is all over the state when not in breeding season.

title: Letter: It's a duck
description: Randy Neal re Cannon Beach infrastructure spending
content:
We know the old saying about looking and quacking like a duck … it's a duck!
The city of Cannon Beach has worked hard to avoid calling its $33.6 million borrowing a bond. They insist it's just a financing agreement!

title: Astoria police conduct crosswalk enforcement to promote pedestrian safety
author: Jasmine Lewin The Astorian
description: Astoria police conducted crosswalk enforcement on Thursday to draw attention to pedestrian safety.
content:
Astoria police conducted crosswalk enforcement on Thursday to draw attention to pedestrian safety.
The initiative is funded by Oregon Impact, which promotes safe driving and offers grants to police departments for traffic safety improvements.

title: North Tillamook Library Friends hold book sale
author: The Astorian
description: MANZANITA — The North Tillamook Library Friends Book Sale, with more than 6,000 used books, takes place in three locations from 5 to 7 p.m. on Friday for current members
content:
MANZANITA — The North Tillamook Library Friends Book Sale, with more than 6,000 used books, takes place in three locations from 5 to 7 p.m. on Friday for current members and opens to the public from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Saturday.
Fiction and children's books are at the Pine Grove Community House on Laneda Avenue. Nonfiction books are at the Hoffman Center for the Arts on Laneda Avenue and at the Fellowship Hall of the Calvary Bible Church on Laneda Avenue.

title: Behind the News: 'This feels like the last option'
author: Derrick De Pledge The Astorian
description: Cannon Beach Together formed in April to challenge the City Council's decision to move forward on a $33.6 million bond for a new City Hall and police station and the
content:
Cannon Beach Together formed in April to challenge the City Council's decision to move forward on a $33.6 million bond for a new City Hall and police station and the redevelopment of a former elementary school.
The political action committee describes itself as a community watchdog for prudent and fiscally responsible governance. The main goal is to force a vote on whether the city should issue the bond.

title: Weekend Break: 'Works of love'
author: Patrick Webb
description: Christine Trexel had experience sewing, doing needlepoint and bookbinding, but when she visited an Ilwaco museum show she resolved to embrace another fiber art: rug hooking.
content:
C hristine Trexel had experience sewing, doing needlepoint and bookbinding, but when she visited an Ilwaco museum show she resolved to embrace another fiber art: rug hooking.
The exhibit is called 'Walking On Art: Traditional Hooked Rugs of the Ocean Park Rug Club 1974-2024.'
Patrick Webb is a former managing editor of The Astorian.

title: Guest Column: Unsafe conditions threaten behavioral health workforce
author: Porter Clements
description: Every year about this time, Oregon labor unions honor colleagues who have lost their lives on the job. This year is especially poignant for members of the American Federation of
content:
Every year about this time, Oregon labor unions honor colleagues who have lost their lives on the job. This year is especially poignant for members of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, or Oregon AFSCME, with the death late last year of Haley Rogers, a 26-year-old mental health worker.
She was stabbed to death on the job by a resident while working an overnight shift alone at a 10-bed behavioral health treatment facility in Gresham. Her death was preventable, and we must ensure that nothing like it happens again.
Porter Clements is president of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Local 1790 and a bilingual outreach and enrollment specialist at Outside In, a Portland-based health care and social services agency that works with homeless youth.

title: In One Ear: Hooligans
author: Elleda Wilson The Astorian
description: Those naughty orcas off Southwest Europe have struck again, Euronews Green reports. On May 12, they repeatedly rammed a 49-foot sailing yacht in the Strait of Gibraltar until it sank.
content:
Those naughty orcas off Southwest Europe have struck again, Euronews Green reports. On May 12, they repeatedly rammed a 49-foot sailing yacht in the Strait of Gibraltar until it sank. The two aboard were luckily rescued by a nearby oil tanker.
The same small pod of about 15 killer whales, designated as Gladis, is responsible. Grupo Trabajo Orca Atlántica, a research group that tracks the subspecies, says there have been hundreds of such orca/boat interactions with the pod since 2020, but only three boats have sunk.

title: Runolfson serves at Navy helicopter squadron in Japan
author: The Astorian
description: Airman Recruit Brandon Runolfson, of Hammond, serves in the U.S. Navy as an aviation electrician's mate in Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron 12 in Japan.
content:
Airman Recruit Brandon Runolfson, of Hammond, serves in the U.S. Navy as an aviation electrician's mate in Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron 12 in Japan.
Runolfson graduated from Warrenton High School in 2023 and joined the Navy a year ago. "I joined because my grandpa was a career Navy man,' he said. "I wanted to follow in his footsteps. I looked up to him, and I thought it would be a good way to see the world."

title: Huacuja maintains lead over Scheller as more ballots counted in county commission race
author: The Astorian
description: Anthony Huacuja has maintained his lead over Tessa Scheller in the District 2 race for the Clatsop County Board of Commissioners as more ballots were counted.
content:
Anthony Huacuja has maintained his lead over Tessa Scheller in the District 2 race for the Clatsop County Board of Commissioners as more ballots were counted.
After an update Thursday, Huacuja led Scheller 50% to 49%, or 1,122 to 1,094, a slightly tighter split than late Tuesday night.

title: Volunteer Notes: May 23, 2024
description: Volunteer opportunities

title: Letter: Together
description: Kaydence Knapp re Knappa High School
content:
As I reflect on my educational journey at Knappa High School, I am reminded of the profound impact a small class of students can have on one's life. In a world where impersonal megaclassrooms are becoming the norm, I feel fortunate to have experienced the warmth and camaraderie of a small, close-knit class.
In our small class, we were more than just classmates — we were a family. We shared laughter, tears and memories that will last a lifetime. Our teachers, who doubled as mentors and role models, fostered an environment of trust, support and encouragement. Together, we navigated the ups and downs of academic and personal struggles, celebrating each other's triumphs and lifting each other up during difficult times.

content:
Since wedding season is upon us, mention should be made of a Cannon Beach History Center and Museum Instagram post featuring a long-gone coastal landmark, the Wedding Tree.
The tree was officially declared dead in 1963, and disappeared sometime in the 1980s. According to a July 1974 article in the Seaside Signal: 'The Indian Wedding Tree stands at the foot of Adams Street in Cannon Beach. Legend has it that area Native Americans were married under its drooping branches, which formed a ring around the couple. Now weather-beaten and deteriorating, the tree holds its ground precariously.'

title: Letter: Good governance?
description: Julia Snyder re proposed timber harvest
content:
As a resident of Sylvandale Lane, across the road from homeowners who will be directly impacted by the proposed Davis Ridge clearcut, I can take a very small step back from the concerns of those neighbors. In doing so, I see just how broad an impact that clearcut will have.
Chemical sprays could be used to destroy undergrowth to keep it from slowing the development of new sapling roots. During the rainy season, those chemicals would be carried by sediment down slopes along Aldrich Point Road and into Gnat Creek. That sediment would reduce stream size and, together with the chemicals, endanger the salmon. Both would ultimately impact the watershed that provides our drinking water.

title: Letter: Save Davis Ridge
description: Denise Moore re proposed timber harvests
content:
I am writing to express my concern about the proposed harvest by the Oregon Department of Forestry of Davis Ridge, which has been our boundary for the past 34 years. The planned logging activities threaten the environment, local biodiversity and community health.
Davis Ridge hosts a diverse array of plant and animal species that rely on the mature forest ecosystem. Logging will disrupt this habitat, causing loss of biodiversity and displacing species. Davis Ridge is home to pileated woodpeckers, bald eagles, spotted owl, great horned owl, turkey vultures and a complex web of beings that live there, and will be threatened by the proposed harvest.

title: Letter: Enormous
description: Dale Flowers re campaign finance
content:
If you or I, or any of our relatives, neighbors and friends pursued a political career, it would take substantial amounts of cash to run a successful campaign. This is especially true at the federal level. Even at the state level, those amounts have become enormous.
And, the biggest donors are corporations. Whenever a legislator votes on a bill, they are forever looking over their shoulder to make sure they don't offend their biggest donors. Does it come as any surprise that the average citizen feels as if the government does not adequately represent their interests first?

title: Dispatch team receives award
author: The Astorian
description: The Astoria Police Department has announced that the Oregon Chapter of the Association of Public Safety Communications Officials — National Emergency Number Association has awarded Dispatchers Jodie Frost and Amber
content:
The Astoria Police Department has announced that the Oregon Chapter of the Association of Public Safety Communications Officials — National Emergency Number Association has awarded Dispatchers Jodie Frost and Amber Easterbrook, Operations Supervisor Candace Pozdolski and Communications Manager Jeremy Hipes the Commitment to Excellence Award. The award recognizes a group of telecommunicators who have demonstrated commitment to the principles of excellence in
911 telecommunications by: Dedication to the profession; creative and innovative approaches to quality improvement; promotion of the Telecommunicator Code of Ethics by example; and leadership and mentoring of co-workers. Closed and consolidated with the Seaside Dispatch Center in 2021, Astoria Dispatch returned to Astoria in March 2022, with the addition of Jeremy Hipes, and the certification of Amber Easterbrook. In fall 2022, three police officers and a firefighter were trained to answer non-emergency calls. Over the following six months, the team undertook a series of initiatives by revamping the training program and hiring practices, updating the policies, introducing new or updated software and fostering a culture of dedication. They monitored two police and three fire channels, answering almost 6,000 phone calls a month, entering nearly 20,000 calls for service and averaging over 100 hours of overtime per month.

content:

Circle Creek stretches more than 300 acres across the flood plain of the Necanicum River. The nonprofit purchased the land 20 years ago and has worked on replanting tens of thousands of native plants in the area since. Bonamici, who has visited with the land conservancy several times over the years, has seen the difference that work has made in mitigating flooding on U.S. Highway 101.

title: Letter: Our beloved libraries
description: Mary Blake re Recall drive in Seaside

For anyone making their way through this most amazing journey called life, one must be curious and open to other peoples' stories. Stories connect us, and help us find our way or make our way.

title: Cedar and Sea Exhibit at Columbia River Maritime Museum
description: Coming this October to the Columbia River Maritime Museum, patrons will have the rare opportunity to learn about the maritime culture of the Indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest Coast
content:

For centuries, the native people of the Pacific Coast have used a deep knowledge of their surrounding environment to harvest its natural wealth, developing sophisticated technologies that enabled them to create and maintain some of North America's most complex and rich cultures, from Yakutat, Alaska, to Canada and down the coast to California.

author: Elleda Wilson The Astorian
description: A whale tale: On July 23, a humpback whale breached just a few feet from the stern of a fiberglass fishing boat off Portsmouth, New Hampshire, flipping and swamping the
content:
A whale tale: On July 23, a humpback whale breached just a few feet from the stern of a fiberglass fishing boat off Portsmouth, New Hampshire, flipping and swamping the boat and unceremoniously dumping the two fishermen aboard into the drink, Maritime-Executive reports.
Fortunately, teenagers Colin and Wyatt Yager were nearby, and were able to rescue the fishermen and get them into another boat so they could go ashore. The fishermen were fine, but wet, the whale also appeared to be OK after its misadventure, the boat was recovered and the incident was reported to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

title: Smokey Bear Celebrates 80th Birthday
author: The Ad Council
description: America's beloved wildfire prevention icon and the longest-running PSA campaign is recognized nationwide for eight decades of impact
content:
America's beloved wildfire prevention icon and the longest-running PSA campaign is recognized nationwide for eight decades of impact
WASHINGTON, Aug. 9, 2024 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, Smokey Bear celebrates eight decades of educating Americans about the role they play in preventing unwanted human-caused wildfires. From his origins during World War II when fears of incendiary shells led to his emergence as a symbol of fire prevention, Smokey's "Only You" message has since become ingrained into American culture through thousands of posters, radio ads, TV spots, billboards, and merchandise. To honor 80 years of Smokey Bear, the USDA Forest Service (USFS), the National Association of State Foresters (NASF), FCB New York and the Ad Council are inviting the public to join Smokey's birthday celebrations and be part of his wildfire prevention legacy.

title: In One Ear: Shrouded ships
author: Elleda Wilson The Astorian
description: Since 1800, the Graveyard of the Pacific, which ranges from Tillamook Bay to Vancouver Island, British Columbia, has claimed more than 2,000 vessels, according to historylink.org, with more than 700
content:
Since 1800, the Graveyard of the Pacific, which ranges from Tillamook Bay to Vancouver Island, British Columbia, has claimed more than 2,000 vessels, according to historylink.org, with more than 700 lives lost just around the Columbia River Bar. The exact location of many of the ships is still shrouded in mystery.
But that's where the Maritime Archaeological Society, a citizen scientist nonprofit organization, comes in. They are dedicated to finding lost shipwrecks. 'Our targets include the wreck of a Spanish galleon, historic steamers and sailing ships along the Oregon Coast and into the Puget Sound,' Chris Dewey, the executive director of the society, explained. They also want to locate and repatriate historical Native American canoes that have been swallowed in river mud.

content:
It was another sad day for representative government in Clatsop County on Aug. 7, when Clatsop County's Board of Commissioners decided to proceed with new amendments to the county's Land and Water Development and Use Code, geared toward fast-tracking housing development and drastically reducing public involvement.
Ignoring 25 letters communicating opposition to the amendments submitted by impacted residents and other concerned parties, one letter including 60 residents' signatures, the commissioners in record time green-lighted these ill-conceived and premature land use code changes.

title: Letter: Far from over
description: Michael Kalkofen re global immunizations
content:
For millions of children, immunizations can make the difference between a life of poverty and one of possibility. When kids are protected from infectious diseases, they can go to school, their parents can go to work and their communities can thrive. Over the past two decades, the world has made astounding progress immunizing children, thanks in large part to Gavi, The Vaccine Alliance.
Since 2000, Gavi has helped prevent 17.3 million deaths by helping countries ensure children receive vaccines to protect them from diseases like measles, cholera, HPV, ebola and — most recently — malaria. But make no mistake — the fight to ensure no child dies of a preventable disease is far from over. Eighty-five million children missed a routine dose during the COVID-19 pandemic, driving surges of preventable diseases like measles, which saw deaths rise by 43% between 2021 and 2022.

title: Letter: Turn the page
description: Carol Merwin re political climate
content:
"We are not enemies, but friends. We must not be enemies. Though passion may have strained it must not break our bonds of affection. The mystic chords of memory, stretching from every battlefield and patriot grave to every living heart and hearthstone all over this broad land, will yet swell the chorus of the Union, when again touched, as surely they will be, by the better angels of our nature." Those words are from President Abraham Lincoln.
After years that have brought forward an ugly and divisive political climate, it appears we are starting to see the better side of our nature. I say that because crowd sizes are diminishing, and people are walking out on political speeches that focus on negativity and a litany of grievances, that are filled with insult after insult and lie after lie.

The county's Ambulance Service Area Advisory Committee convened with Medix owner J.D. Fuiten and general manager Thomas Krokoski for a special meeting on Tuesday to discuss those frustrations.

title: Letter: Unchecked debt
description: Lisa Nofield re Cannon Beach Elementary School redevelopment
content:
Together, let's vote "no" on ballot Measure 4-234, the proposed $12-million luxury tourist facility. The city's three projects, totaling $33.6 million, is excessive for our small village. The 30-year debt, combined with interest, is approximately $60 million.

title: Extra fishing days added on river
author: The Astorian
description: Oregon and Washington state fisheries managers have added an extra two weeks for Chinook salmon retention on the main stem Columbia River.
content:
Oregon and Washington state fisheries managers have added an extra two weeks for Chinook salmon retention on the main stem Columbia River.
Chinook retention will now remain open in the Buoy 10 fishery through Oct. 13 with a daily adult bag limit of three salmon (Chinook or hatchery coho, only one may be a Chinook). From Oct. 14 to Oct. 31, three adult hatchery coho can be retained daily, but Chinook must be released.

title: Student test scores on the North Coast remain stagnant
author: Rebecca Norden-Bright
description: County, state schools still recovering from pandemic-era learning loss
content:
Students in Clatsop County and across Oregon are still struggling to recover from pandemic-era learning loss, according to the latest Oregon State Assessment System scores.
The state Department of Education released results for all school districts on Thursday. Students in third-through-eighth grades and in 11th grade are tested each spring in math and language arts, although testing was waived for two years during the coronavirus pandemic. Students in fifth, eighth and 11th grades are tested in science.

content:
The pilot schooner J. C. Cousins, once a luxury yacht, then a Columbia River bar pilot boat, was competing with Capt. title: Letter: Unfit for City Council
description: John Windus re Mimi Rose's campaign for Astoria City Council
content:
I've learned two things from my experiences interacting with the city of Astoria and the Astoria City Council: The first is that city staff is professional and reasonable when serving the public. The second is that every vote on the City Council matters. When I had business before the council, even though Councilor Tom Hilton and I disagreed, I appreciated his request for civility in public discourse.
The social media posts by one of the candidates running to replace Hilton in Ward 4 have been particularly concerning. Mimi Rose has attacked those who disagree with her views on affordable housing as being "mentally challenged." She has suggested forming "a picket line" in front of LiFEBoat Services and dehumanizes LiFEBoat's clients by calling it a "feeding station." She says the unhoused deserve a "one way bus ticket to where they came from" even though many seeking services are from here. Rose demeans others while calling herself "one of the few & brave who own a building Downtown to keep it running for unappreciative citizens like you."

author: Elleda Wilson
description: The largest ocean liner constructed in the U.S., the SS United States, only sailed for 17 years, but still holds its 1952 title for the fastest Atlantic crossing by a
content:
The largest ocean liner constructed in the U.S., the SS United States, only sailed for 17 years, but still holds its 1952 title for the fastest Atlantic crossing by a passenger ship. Retired in 1969, the once iconic ship has fallen on hard times.
It's been a long and often ugly battle, but the former luxury cruise liner has finally found a new home. That's only after wrangling in and out of court over rent and possible eviction with the pier company owners in Philadelphia, where the ship has been docked and deteriorating since 1996, Maritime Executive reports.

description: A history gem from The Daily Morning Astorian, Oct. 16, 1885 issue is the article, 'Early Settlers and Settlements on Clatsop Plain.' Included are stories told by Celiast (aka Helen)
content:
A history gem from The Daily Morning Astorian, Oct. 16, 1885 issue is the article, 'Early Settlers and Settlements on Clatsop Plain.' Included are stories told by Celiast (aka Helen) Coboway Smith (1801-1891), daughter of Chief Coboway, and wife of Solomon Howard Smith (her second husband). The couple are pictured.
With her son Silas B. Smith interpreting, she repeated the oral tradition of how the Clatsops came to settle on the North Coast. Tahlipas, 'a great and superior being,' brought her tribe the plain, she said, and gave the land to them.

Recently, Portland has had an unusual visitor, but those in the know 'aren't sure' what it is, Oregon Public Broadcasting reports. Nevertheless, it looks like an Arctic white fox.

title: Weekend Break: Clamming under a crescent moon
description: Calm seas, clear skies and abundant clams.
content:
C alm seas, clear skies and abundant clams.
The first round of recreational razor clam digs for the fall season commenced in early October on Oregon and Washington state beaches.
Along the Long Beach Peninsula, an estimated 4,800 diggers participated over the first five days.
Clatsop County beaches, which account for about 90% of Oregon's razor clam harvest, reopened to clamming on Oct. 1 after a conservation closure that began July 15. Beaches in southwest Washington reopened on Oct. 3.
'We fortunately had really nice digging conditions this whole first tide series with calm seas and dry weather, resulting in mostly limits from everyone we encountered,' said Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife coastal shellfish biologist Bryce Blumenthal.
Buy Now
Clammers in the surf near Seaview, Washington, with North Head Lighthouse shining in the background.
Luke Whittaker/Chinook Observer
'Clear skies and a crescent moon allowed for diggers to enjoy a beautiful sky full of stars the past couple nights. I think the rain Friday resulted in lower turnout, even though it was dry and calm by the time low tide occurred in the evening.'
The next series of recreational clam digs on the peninsula is slated through Monday, with evening low tides of -0.8 to -1.7 feet between 8 and 11 p.m. over the weekend. That comes after tests proved toxin levels are within the safe range for consumption.
The Washington Department of Health requires test samples for marine toxins, and domoic acid levels must fall under the guideline level before a beach can open for digging. Final approval usually occurs about a week or less — sometimes two to three days — before the start of each digging series.

Domoic acid levels in clam meat in Long Beach, Washington, have remained below the threshold of 20 parts per million since last exceeding the limit in February 2023. The highest domoic acid levels on record in Long Beach occurred in October 2002, when levels reached 132 parts per million. The most recent test this fall showed a level of 2 ppm.
Rules in Oregon and Washington state require each digger to keep their first 15 clams, regardless of size or condition, in their own separate container.
The Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife compiles a thorough annual report on past clam seasons and what to expect in the year ahead.
The recent survey found an average of 0.84 clams per square meter along the beach between Long Beach and Ocean Park. The highest density of clams was near Oysterville and at the top of the peninsula, with around 2 to 2.5 per square meter.
Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife reckons the total number of adult clams — 3 inches or more — this year on the peninsula is about 6 million, nearly identical to last year's estimate. The total estimated harvest last year was about 1.5 million, or 69% of the allowable quota. This year's quota is just over 2.1 million.
The average size of adult Long Beach clams found in the 2024 surveys was 3.87 inches.
Meanwhile, over the summer, Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife biologists found juvenile recruitment to be down significantly from the 20-year average.

title: Letter: Truly represent
description: Jan Mitchell re Astoria City Councilor Andy Davis for state House
content:
Before moving to Astoria 30 years ago, I worked for a city that enacted developers' fees. Our candidates for state representative in House District 32 differ on this issue, with state Rep. Cyrus Javadi criticizing Astoria City Councilor Andy Davis for supporting Astoria's fee structure. Let's be clear; either new development pays for needed infrastructure, or existing taxpayers do. That means you.
There are many differences between these candidates, including their positions on women's health and the primacy of clean water in coastal communities. title: Letter: Blazingly obvious
description: Dan Hubner re housing
content:
I was genuinely surprised and baffled to read that Ward 4 City Council candidate, Lisa Morley, is advocating for no more housing to be built in Astoria (" Divisions emerge among Astoria City Council candidates at forum," Oct. 17). To be blunt, the idea that affordability can be addressed without more housing is ridiculous and unserious.
Refusing to build housing won't stop people from moving to Astoria, it will just ensure that only the wealthiest can afford to buy what housing exists. This is not a hypothetical problem for the future, it is a currently-existing one. A home in Astoria (at least, one without major expensive structural defects on top of the purchase price) is already pretty much out of reach even for middle-class families, and if you're working class, forget about it.

title: Letter: Demonstrates
description: At the Cannon Beach Coffee with the Councilors Oct. 21, a comment made by City Council candidate Mike Bates needs to be corrected. Bates stated that the Cannon Beach Chamber

At the Cannon Beach Coffee with the Councilors Oct. 21, a comment made by City Council candidate Mike Bates needs to be corrected. Bates stated that the Cannon Beach Chamber of Commerce receives 70% of the transient lodging funds. This misinformation on how funds are dispersed demonstrates a complete lack of understanding of the subject.
The Chamber of Commerce is a nonprofit organization with the mission of supporting the business community of Cannon Beach. It receives no funding from the city but is funded by member dues. The chamber is contracted by the city of Cannon Beach to provide visitor information and destination marketing within the chamber-owned building. According to the city budget, this contact is funded by 7% of the total TLT funds collected and remitted to the city from hotel revenue. This contract was supported by the lodging industry when the city increased the lodging tax in 2015. Annually, the chamber receives approximately $500,000 to do this work.

title: Weekend Break: 'Battlegrounds and Backroads'
author: Mike Francis
description: Sean Davis and Brad Pietzyk have personal reasons for wanting you to think about veterans who take their own lives.
content:
Sean Davis and Brad Pietzyk have personal reasons for wanting you to think about veterans who take their own lives.
The Astoria men, both veterans of overseas combat deployments, have been suicidal themselves. And they've lost friends who decided it was better to end their pain than to go on living.
They have come to grips with some sorrowful facts: Oregon has a pronounced veteran suicide problem. The state has a significantly higher rate of suicide among military veterans than most — more than 46% higher than the national rate in 2021, according to the Department of Veterans Affairs. And the rate of Oregon veteran suicides is more than 2 1/2 times higher than the national rate of suicide among all people, including nonveterans.
In 2021, the last year a full dataset has been reported, 139 veterans in Oregon took their lives. They ranged in age from teenagers to people older than 75.
Why is this? Those who have studied this disparity note that Oregon has no full-time, active-duty military installation in the state. Instead, military veterans — many of them former members of the National Guard — are scattered in communities throughout the state, with limited forms of support, whether emotional, financial or medical.
Portions of 'Battlegrounds and Backgrounds' will be shown at the Ten Fifteen Theater in Astoria on Veterans Day. The two filmmakers hope to show the project around the state.
They may be isolated, they may be drinking or taking drugs to self-medicate, they may have crumbling personal relationships, or all three. And all have familiarity with — and usually access to — firearms, which were used in more than 70% of Oregon's veteran suicides in 2021.
For Pietzyk, the brush with death came after he returned to his home in Alaska from his second deployment to Iraq, where he commanded a U.S. Army engineering support unit. He was single, lonely and isolated. Also, he said, 'I started having mental issues.'
One day, he was sitting in a chair at home, a rifle across his lap. He thinks he was moments from aiming it at himself and pulling the trigger when his dog, a 'very intuitive' husky-shepherd mix, placed its head on his knee.
That small action snapped him back, he said, buying him a few seconds — seconds that 'may have saved my life.' He medically retired in 2017 and lives on disability with his wife and children in Astoria.
Davis was riding in a military vehicle in Iraq when it was struck by a blast from a bomb-laden car. He suffered life-threatening injuries and was medevaced to a military hospital in Germany, where his long road to recovery began. After years of cycling through medical treatments and the military bureaucracy, he began to think he was too big a burden on the people who cared about him. He drank increasing volumes of alcohol, even vowing one new year to drink heavily every day of the coming year.
He made it to Easter, when he awoke at 3 a.m. and found himself studying the desiccated Christmas tree that still stood in the house he shared with roommates. He dragged it to the yard, clicked his Zippo, and the tree went up in a flash, rousing neighbors and causing a roommate to rush out and douse the blaze.
Intro subscription only $1.99
To this day, he can't explain why he did it. 'Maybe I needed a big moment,' he said. 'I'm not even sure.'
The next day, he visited an American Legion representative and started working on his disability claim. After it was approved and his finances stabilized, he went on to earn three degrees, including a master's of fine arts from Pacific University. He is now married and lives in Astoria with his wife and daughter.
'We both could have been a statistic,' Pietzyk said.
Davis, a creative dynamo who has written a memoir called 'The Wax Bullet War' and other books, is a talented artist and a writing tutor at Clatsop Community College.
He and Pietzyk have become close, and together they conceived the notion of creating a documentary to call attention to the state's plague of veteran suicide.
They were awarded a grant by the nonprofit Together With Veterans and have completed one road trip through parts of the state, conducting interviews with a variety of people, from elected officials to veterans in rural towns. They will launch on a second trip two days after the screening at the Ten Fifteen Theater.
A key problem they've focused on has been the loss of purpose that many veterans feel after coming home and separating from their friends and comrades. They may be physically well, and they may be financially stable, but they are no longer grounded in a team with a shared mission.
Davis and Pietzyk created a program called Help Enhance Rural Oregon, or HERO, and have enlisted Mike Neelon of the Clatsop County Emergency Management Department to pilot it in Clatsop County.
Neelon will help spread the word to veterans when he learns of volunteer opportunities, such as helping to respond to emergencies, and he will invite them to emergency response training events. The pilot program is intended to help veterans find ways to plug into their communities, and it will be explored in the documentary.
When 'Battlegrounds and Backroads' is finished, the Astoria veterans hope to show it around the state. Davis said people should be surprised to learn how broad and troubling the phenomenon of veteran suicide is, especially in Oregon.
Said Davis, 'We want to show why, how and what can we do to stop this.'
New documentary
New documentary
Portions of 'Battlegrounds and Backroads,' a forthcoming documentary about suicide among veterans in rural Oregon, will be shown 6:30 p.m. Monday at the Ten Fifteen Theater, 1015 Commercial St., Astoria.
The showing is free, with donations encouraged to help complete the project.

title: In One Ear: 'A special joy'
author: Elleda Wilson
description: 'She did it again!' the Pacific Region for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service announced Dec. 3 on their X page. 'She' is Wisdom, a Laysan albatross, and the world's
content:
'She did it again!' the Pacific Region for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service announced Dec. 3 on their X page. 'She' is Wisdom, a Laysan albatross, and the world's oldest-known wild bird at the age of approximately 74.
She returns to Midway Atoll each year to reunite with her mate and, hopefully, lay one egg. The 'Queen of Seabirds' has a new partner (her decadeslong partner, Akeakamai, disappeared several years ago), and she has laid yet another egg — her first in four years. Wisdom (left) and her new partner are pictured.

title: In One Ear: Hold the fort
author: Elleda Wilson The Astorian
description: Did you know that 219 years ago, the Lewis and Clark Corps of Discovery was in the throes of building Fort Clatsop? They started construction on Dec. 9, 1805.
content:
Did you know that 219 years ago, the Lewis and Clark Corps of Discovery was in the throes of building Fort Clatsop? They started construction on Dec. 9, 1805.
The Oregon Encyclopedia describes the fort as consisting of two cabins, with a parade ground between them that had gates on each end. One cabin had three rooms for the enlisted men. The other contained a room for the captains, one for the Charbonneaus (Sacagawea and family), an orderly room and a storeroom. On Christmas Day, the corps moved in.
